documents.abstract: Introduction Strategic and organizational solutions are becoming essential due to the global demand for digital transformation, sustained operational efficiency, and the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence adoption on organizational efficiency, with digital literacy as a boundary condition and organizational learning capability serving as a mediator. Methods The study utilized a quantitative cross-sectional survey-based design. A multistage sampling technique was used to collect data from employees working in the Ghanaian banking sector. Data collected from 388 employees from the banks were utilized in an empirical study employing structural equation modeling. Both direct and indirect relationships were assessed. Results The findings revealed that the level of artificial intelligence adoption has a significant and positive influence on both organizational efficiency and organizational learning capability. The results further showed that organizational learning capability has a significant and positive influence on organizational efficiency and partially mediates the relationship between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency. Additionally, the results revealed that digital literacy moderates the relationships between artificial intelligence adoption and organizational efficiency, as well as the relationships between organizational learning capability and organizational efficiency. Conclusion This study introduces a novel theoretical framework that connects the hitherto overlooked linkages between artificial intelligence adoption, organizational learning capability, digital literacy, and organizational efficiency within the banking sector of an emerging economy. By integrating these constructs into a unified model, the study clarifies the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI adoption translates into organizational efficiency, thereby extending the Resource-Based View in an emerging-market context.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing audit practice by expanding analytical coverage, automating routine procedures, and supporting more continuous risk assessment. These benefits, however, also raise questions about accountability, explainability, professional judgment, data protection, and legal responsibility. This study examines whether AI auditability and oversight design shape assurance professionals’ perceptions of ethical risk, legal exposure, and audit quality in Ghana. Using a quantitative design, the study combines a cross-sectional survey of 180 assurance professionals with a between-subjects vignette experiment. AI auditability was assessed in terms of data traceability, model documentation, explainability, governance controls, role clarity, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) procedures. The experiment compared manual-only auditing, AI-only auditing, and AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. AI auditability was negatively associated with perceived ethical risk (β = −0.456, p < .001) and positively associated with perceived audit quality (β = 0.424, p < .001). Perceived ethical risk was positively associated with perceived legal exposure (β = 0.536, p < .001) and negatively associated with perceived audit quality (β = −0.268, p < .001). Although AI auditability was negatively correlated with perceived legal exposure, its direct regression effect was not statistically significant after ethical risk was controlled (β = −0.092, p = .392). The experiment showed that AI-only oversight was associated with higher perceptions of ethical and legal risk than AI-assisted auditing with HITL oversight. Because the study measures professional perceptions rather than observed legal events or realized audit outcomes, the findings should be interpreted as evidence about perceived risk and quality. Overall, the results indicate that responsible AI adoption in auditing depends less on automation alone than on auditable governance, meaningful human oversight, and clear accountability.

documents.abstract: Abstract In the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the field of Library and Information Science is evolving rapidly with the introduction of new paradigms in information management, information discovery, and service delivery. This is a conceptual paper that analyses the role of AI and its future implications on the library and information services. It examines key AI technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, chatbots, robotics, AI-powered discovery services, personalized information services and generative AI, and explores how these are being used in modern libraries. This paper emphasises the benefits of these technologies in information retrieval, automating repetitive library functions, delivering personalized services to users, facilitating research activities, and engaging users. It also looks at how technology is evolving like smart libraries and AI-driven information services. Meanwhile, the paper covers important challenges that must be addressed in the context of the adoption of AI, such as privacy, data security, algorithmic bias, misinformation, copyright, ethical issues, technological costs, and technical skills. The evolving nature of the role of LIS professionals and the skills needed to collaborate with emerging AI technologies are given special attention. The paper proposes that AI is not the end of librarians but an enabler and a supportive tool for librarians. By combining AI with professional knowledge, ethical considerations, and human-centred services, libraries can become smarter, more efficient, user-friendly, and responsive to user needs. The study highlights the need for responsible use of AI, ongoing professional growth, and collaboration between technology and human skills to shape the future of library services. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an established part of how organizations run their operations, from customer interaction and demand forecasting to logistics, marketing, and knowledge work. This paper examines what that means for global business operations through a documentary case study of Amazon. The study does not collect primary data or measure Amazon's performance independently. It analyzes publicly available sources: Amazon's corporate publications and regulatory filings, reports from international institutions, and peer-reviewed research. The paper keeps a clear line between what Amazon reports having deployed and what independent evidence shows about outcomes. The paper finds that AI can support productivity, personalization, forecasting, automation, and human decision support, but that the effects are neither automatic nor uniform. Drawing on independent studies, it notes that productivity gains can be substantial for some workers, particularly less-experienced ones, while AI can reduce performance on tasks outside its effective capability range. Amazon illustrates how AI can be integrated across a value chain, including recommendations, fulfilment and robotics, demand forecasting, and generative-AI services. The case also shows why adoption needs governance, workforce development, data management, risk assessment, and human oversight. The paper concludes with an eight-step framework for responsible enterprise AI adoption. It starts from a defined business problem, evaluates AI at the level of individual tasks, and draws on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework for risk management. It argues that the value of AI depends less on the technology itself than on organizational readiness and the quality of human-AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: Abstract AI and ML are rapidly changing higher education by redefining teaching, learning, research, evaluation, and institutional governance. India's National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisions a transdisciplinary, technology-enabled, learner-centric, and innovation-driven education system that produces globally competent graduates who can contribute to Viksit Bharat 2047. Despite rising acceptance of AI-based educational technology, equitable access, faculty preparedness, ethical governance, digital infrastructure, and curriculum revision for future workforce needs remain problems. This study critically investigates how AI and ML might improve the quality, accessibility, inclusivity, and effectiveness of higher education in India within NEP 2020. It examines the transformative potential of AI-enabled adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring, predictive learning analytics, automated assessment, academic administration, and research support, using a doctrinal and analytical research methodology grounded in policy documents, government reports, and contemporary academic literature. It also highlights algorithmic unfairness, data privacy, cybersecurity, digital inequality, academic integrity, and ethical issues in the implementation of generative AI. The Competency-Based AI Integration Framework (AI-HE 2047 Framework) integrates digital literacy, critical thinking, interdisciplinary learning, research and innovation, ethical AI governance, and lifelong learning competencies to align AI adoption with the goals of NEP 2020. The methodology helps higher education institutions produce AI-ready graduates for an innovation-driven knowledge economy. The study found that responsible integration of AI and ML, supported by policy reforms, faculty capacity building, institutional readiness, and ethical governance mechanisms, can improve educational quality, employability, research excellence, and India's transition to a knowledge-powered economy under Viksit Bharat 2047.
